q.intro.text: Forty seven divided by six is seven, with five left over. As one true line: forty seven equals six times seven, plus five.

q.ask.text: Polynomials divide the same way. What is x squared plus five x plus seven, divided by x plus two? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the layout moves first, then the algebra.

e.s0.text: Divide the leading terms. x squared divided by x is x. That is the first quotient term, written above the x column.

e.s1.text: Multiply x by the whole divisor: x times x plus two is x squared plus two x. Subtract it. The x squared terms cancel, and three x plus seven is left.

e.s2.text: Repeat with three x plus seven. Three x divided by x is three. Then three times x plus two is three x plus six, and three x plus seven, minus three x plus six, is one.

e.s3.text: One has degree zero, below the degree of the divisor: stop. So x squared plus five x plus seven equals x plus two, times x plus three, plus one. Divided by x plus two, that is x plus three, plus one over x plus two, for x not equal to negative two.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why does the division stop at one?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. A finished remainder has lower degree than the divisor. No term times x plus two can cancel a constant.

e.w-int.text: Size is the whole number rule. For polynomials the test is degree. One has degree zero, and x plus two has degree one.

e.w-zero.text: A division does not have to come out even. Once the degree is below the degree of the divisor, what is left is the remainder.

t.intro.text: Now the shortcut for a divisor like x minus two: synthetic division. The same numbers as long division, without the x s. Divide x cubed minus seven x plus nine by x minus two.

t.setup.text: Done for you. c is two, in the box. The top row is one, zero, negative seven, nine, with a zero for the missing x squared. Bring down the one. Two times one is two, and zero plus two is two.

t.next.text: Your step. Multiply the newest bottom entry by two, and add it to negative seven. What goes in the bottom row?

t.n-ok.text: Yes. Two times two is four, and negative seven plus four is negative three.

t.n-sub.text: The tableau adds the product: negative seven plus four.

t.n-rec.text: Multiply the newest bottom entry, two, not the top entry zero.

t.n-no.text: Multiply two by the bottom entry two, then add that to negative seven.

t.last.text: Same move for the last column. Two times negative three, added to nine. What is the last entry?

t.l-ok.text: Yes. Two times negative three is negative six, and nine plus negative six is three.

t.l-sub.text: Add the product, do not subtract it: nine plus negative six.

t.l-rec.text: Multiply the newest bottom entry, negative three, not the top entry negative seven.

t.l-no.text: Two times negative three is negative six. Add it to nine.

t.read.text: The bottom row is one, two, negative three, and in its box, three. Which quotient and remainder does it give?

t.r-ok.text: Yes. The quotient is one degree lower: x squared plus two x minus three. And the boxed three is the remainder. The same as long division.

t.r-deg.text: Dividing a cubic by x minus two gives a quadratic. The first entry goes with x squared, not x cubed.

t.r-rem.text: The last entry is the remainder, fenced off in its box. It is not a coefficient of the quotient.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked x plus three, plus one over x plus two. And you were right: the remainder one is still divided by x plus two.

t.cb-adds.text: At the start you picked x plus four. That adds the remainder one onto the quotient. The one is left over, so it is still divided by x plus two.

t.cb-term.text: At the start you picked x plus seven halves. That divides term by term: x squared by x, and seven by two. A sum is divided as a whole, and the layout does exactly that.

t.cb-none.text: Every division ends the same way. Dividend equals divisor times quotient, plus remainder.

p.intro.text: Kai says: long division is right because that is the rule. Divide, multiply, subtract, repeat. Is that a reason why it works?

p.build.text: Right. Naming the steps is not a reason. Build one: fill each because, with the reason that makes the line true.

p.test.text: Repeating the rule does not show why it is right. Build a real reason, and see.

p.c1.text: Right. Before anything is divided, P equals D times zero, plus P.

p.c2.text: Right. D times Q plus t adds t D to the product, and S minus t D takes the same t D away. The total is still P.

p.c3.text: Right. t is the leading term of S divided by the leading term of D. So t D and S share a leading term, and it cancels.

p.c4.text: Right. The degree drops every step, so it reaches a degree below the degree of D. And the line P equals D Q plus R is still true.

p.no.ex.text: One example that works is not a reason for every polynomial.

p.no.rule.text: That repeats the rule. The question is why the rule gives a true line.

p.no.comp.text: Adding t to Q adds t D to the product. Without paying it back, the line is no longer true.

p.no.zero.text: The residual does not have to reach zero. One was left over in the example.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That is why long division always works. Every step keeps P equals D Q plus S true, and lowers the degree of S. Synthetic division is the same steps, written short.
